utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start with our next witness, just for the record, I would like to point out that, of course, with reference to Exhibit P310, 310, of course, the pages concerning the opinion of the witness about the activity and role of Vladimir Santic on the 15th and 16th of April must be struck off the record. This is in keeping and actually a consequence of our ruling on Thursday. So I'm referring to this document so that we will not take into account anything relating to that particular point. All right. We may now move to our next witness. Good morning. Could you please stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. Thank you. Learned counsel, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you just briefly indicate what your present occupation is and confirm your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I was born on the 27th March, 1963, and at the moment, I work as a business manager for a construction company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you'd completed formal education, sir, what profession did you take up?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I was an army officer. I joined the British army in 1982 and left in 1992 with a rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, sir, in what branch of the army did you serve? Were you army or infantry or which branch?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I was in the infantry, in the heavy infantry. I served in Germany at the point where we still thought there was a threat from the Russians, and I also served in Northern Ireland on two tours as a counter-terrorist officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left the British army, what particular occupation did you follow then?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: For the following two years, I worked in the former Yugoslavia. For the first year, I was working for the British foreign office as a monitor in the European Community Monitoring Mission based in Zagreb, and then for the second year, I worked for Mr. Stoltenberg in the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take up any particular appointment towards the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. For the bulk of my year with the ECMM, I was assigned to the humanitarian section, based in Zagreb but then working across Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Coming to May of 1993, did you perform any specific commission or particular function at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. Between the 3rd and the 12th of May, 1993, I was sent by the headquarters of ECMM, by the deputy head of the political mission, Ole Brix Andersen, down to Central Bosnia, to Vitez and Zenica, to carry out an investigation into what had happened there in the middle of April, particularly on the 16th of April, and I was told to go down and meet with political and military leaders and civilian leaders on both sides of the confrontation line that had been established between the Croats and the Muslims, to talk to them, to ask them what had happened, and to then write a report, and while I was there, also to stress to them that whatever had happened, it was not to happen again because, quite clearly, it was fairly horrific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the first physical contact you'd had with that particular area of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No. In fact, I'd spent the preceding Christmas and New Year based as the ECMM's liaison officer at Kiseljak. So I was the ECMM liaison officer at General Morillon's headquarters then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, firstly, when you undertook this mission in May of 1993, what did you actually do upon arrival? Did you go and inspect any locations or do anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Having arrived, the first thing that I was concerned to do was to build the picture for myself of what had happened. So I met with the ECMM, who were based in Zenica, my own colleagues there; I met with the BritBat, UNPROFOR, who were based just outside Vitez. I collated all of the reports they had written and plotted it on a map to see what had happened and when, according to our own information. On the 4th of May, I accompanied Jean-Pierre Thebault, who was the head of the ECMM mission in Zenica, across to meet Colonel Bob Stewart, the CO of BritBat, and I accompanied them as they went to look around Ahmici, which was not a particularly pleasant thing to do under the circumstances. I spent the next couple of days continuing to collate information, work out for myself what had happened before then, meeting a range of people and interviewing them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say you visited Ahmici; that was an on-site location. What do you recall observing when you visited the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The village was just outside Vitez. It was a village going up on the side of a hill, gently sloping up the side of a hill. It appeared that it had been a mixed village with probably Croatian houses lower down the hill and Muslim houses then stretching up the roads, going up the hill. There was a mosque in the village which had been attacked and the minaret had been blown up. It was characterised by the fact that some of the houses were still occupied, and the people living in the houses came out to look at what was going on, and then the majority of the houses going up the hill had been burnt. Their roofs had obviously been burnt and had collapsed inside the houses. There was some signs that there had been shooting, with bullet holes in the walls, for example. So I think one could characterise this as a village which had been ethnically cleansed, and I'd say that based in light of various other villages that I had seen in Northern Bosnia and Croatia, which had pretty similar characteristics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you carry out any other kind of on-site inspections during that few-day mission that you undertook?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: While I was there, as well as meeting various people, I also visited the Croatian prison in Busovaca. I didn't get a chance to visit the Muslim prison in Zenica, although I think my success rate in getting people released from that prison was better than my success rate in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in addition to those physical inspections, you have mentioned meeting persons. Could you give us an indication of the kind of persons you met and the kind of bodies or authorities they may have represented?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. As I said, during my introduction, I was basically trying to meet the key military and political leaders. So on the Muslim side, I met the mayor of Zenica and the commander and one of his deputy commanders of 3rd Corps, so that was the local Muslim military formation, and also in Zenica, I met a couple of the Croatian Catholic priests who were effectively the local -- well, not the only, but they were certainly people who one could have access to, leaders of the -- in the pastoral sense, of the Croatian population in Zenica. On the other side, I met the mayor of Vitez, I met then Colonel, now General Blaskic, who was the military commander on the Croatian side. I met some of the Muslim military leaders in one of the villages just outside Vitez, and then in Busovaca, I met the imam, so pastoral leader of the Muslim population in Busovaca, a Croat-controlled town, and I met the man who's running the Croatian prison and a number of Croatian policemen in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the methodology of your meetings with these people, and were you accompanied by anybody else when you went to these meetings?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, for every single meeting that I had, I was accompanied either by Eric Friis-Pedersen, who was an ECMM monitor based in Zenica, or by Jean-Pierre Thebault, who was the head of the regional centre in Zenica, and an interpreter. The methodology that I used was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you for a second. Since we are both on the same language channel, I understand we're being a little fast for the interpreting services. So perhaps you can slow down just a bit. Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly, and I apologise to the interpreters. The methodology that I used for my interviews was fairly simple. I explained in each case who I was, that I had been sent from the headquarters of the ECMM in Zagreb specifically to speak to these people. I asked them to explain, in their own words, what had happened on the 16th of April leading up to that and then immediately thereafter. I took with me to each of the meetings a photocopied map of the area and some coloured pens and invited each of the people that I was talking to to explain to me on the map what had happened, which made it far easier to work out when they were describing events where they were, and then to start relating what they were saying to the picture I built up in my mind of where either the ECMM or UNPROFOR had said that things had taken place. Because I was working in each case through an interpreter, as in the courtroom will get it right, there was a delay between what they were saying and then when I was coming back and asking my next question, which gave me a chance to write down what they were saying, in most cases or in many cases, virtually the datum as it was coming from the interpreter. I then used those handwritten notes, typed up to form the basis of the report that I wrote when I got back to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document now, please, Mr. McLeod. Perhaps the exhibit could be shown, please. Can you say whether you recognise that document, Mr. McLeod?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, this looks like a complete copy of the report which I wrote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what format does that report take?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: What one has is my covering letter distributing it, a list of the contents, a one-page summary of my thoughts, having written the report, a note on how I actually produced the report, and then a series of annexes which are my typed notes, sometimes with the odd comment which I added later on, and then as appendices to the annexes, documents which I was given by various people during the meetings. At the back of the report is a table which was the summary which I produced for myself at the beginning of my tour out there of events as noted in the daily reports or weekly reports of either UNPROFOR or ECMM, and at the very back, there's a photocopy of the map which I annexed to the back so that people could, again, just identify where things had taken place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. McLeod, at page 1 of the report document itself, you actually set forth a text containing a number of observations on your part. Could you just briefly talk us through this and indicate upon what bases you drew those conclusions that you included in that report? Again, sir, I would ask you to be mindful of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. The conclusion that I reached was that on the 16th of April, the Croats had launched a coordinated attack against the Muslim villages around Vitez, of Old Vitez, which was the Muslim part of Vitez. At the same time, it appeared that they had arrested 13 leading members of the Muslim community in Vitez --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could interrupt at that point. Did you look into that question of the supposed arrest of 13 persons?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. I was given a list of people whom the Muslims were keen to trace by the mayor of Zenica. I discussed the list with the members of the Muslim military that I met just outside Vitez and they told me what they thought had happened to some of them. I then met a number of men who had been arrested in the prison in Busovaca, and I met one of the men who had been arrested and then released in his house in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you said you made the observation that the Croats launched a coordinated attack. Can you just explain why you drew that particular conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It was quite clear from all of the reports and what I was being told by both parties that early in the morning of the 16th of April, fighting had broken out in a number of places at the same time, and that in itself suggested that there had been a coordinated attack on somebody's behalf. So the issue was then to work out -- I think there was no dispute about the fact that this had taken place, so there was no dispute about the fact that events had started in a number of places at the same time. It was then a matter of working out whether the events had been started by one party or the other party. The most significant event which would suggest that it was started by the Croats rather than by the Muslims was that a number of people were arrested early in the morning in their beds, and having had personal experience of trying to pick people up in Northern Ireland, I'm aware that you have to put quite a lot of thought and effort into going in to collect even one person, as opposed to a number of people. So that event in itself appeared to me to be coordinated, and, therefore, it struck me that if, as the Croats suggested, the Muslims had attacked them and they had been caught completely by surprise, then they would have been defending their positions rather than going out in a coordinated manner and arresting people in their beds. Equally, if the Muslims had launched this coordinated attack against the Croats, then the very people that were arrested would have been at least prepared for this and probably not asleep in their beds. Therefore, my conclusion was that since nobody was disputing the fact that something had been clearly coordinated, that one side was coordinating it and one side was reacting to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke to the various people, however, whom you interviewed, did you get any differing, as it were, theories or schools of thought as to what had actually happened?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. Basically, there were three theories that were going around; two of them one can find fairly easily attributed within the report, the third one clearly I had picked up at that point, although it's not attributed within the report, and those were, first of all, that perhaps the Croats had launched an attack on the Muslims. This was the Muslim point of view. Secondly, that the Muslims had attacked the Croats. This was one of the Croatian points of view, and Colonel Blaskic, for example, said he had been surprised by this attack and woke up in his bed. There was also a theory being put about that it was -- well, Ahmici particularly was actually the work of Serb agent provocateur who were attempting to stir up a conflict between the Croats and the Muslims, but that, frankly, didn't seem to hold much water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have clearly, in your report, opted for one of those versions, so can you just give us an indication as to why you -- what factual grounds you ascertained to discount the others? Firstly, the Serb one, I mean.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: While it was quite clear that the Serbs who had been attacking southwards from Northern Bosnia were against both the Croats and the Muslims for a very long time, were continuing to shell, for example, I think Muslim areas and probably Croat areas before and after these events took place, and therefore they would have been quite happy if they could have found some way of destabilising what, up until then, had been a fairly satisfactory military alliance between the two parties. I find it hard to believe that they could have mounted a series of coordinated, covert attacks and made them look like the work of one or other of the parties without really having realised what was going on. Therefore, as to whether it was a series of Muslim attacks, while the Muslims could clearly have mounted a series of attacks, and indeed there what I would see as their counterattack was very nearly successful, so they had the capability of doing something like that, then I can't believe the Croats would have had the time to go around arresting people in Vitez, amongst other things. Also, for example, having looking at Ahmici, it was quite clear that the battle damage was all to the Muslim houses as opposed to the Croat houses. I think that if the Muslims had been attacking, then it would have been the other way around, and therefore I was left pretty much with the conclusion that I reached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the third paragraph of your observations, you mention movement of Croat population through propaganda. How do you reach that observation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Well, this is based on what I was told by the ECMM, by the UNPROFOR, and indeed by both the mayors of Zenica and Vitez. There was no dispute about the fact that a large proportion of the Muslim population of Zenica had requested and attempted to move from Zenica to Vitez. The overriding impression which I had, having talked particularly with Jean-Pierre Thebault, was that this was something which the Croats were attempting to orchestrate possibly for a couple of reasons; one, to make sure that it would not seem unreasonable when there was a return of Muslim population from the Vitez area, and a number of different reasons all stemming from the same point. But it would also, if there was a movement of population, justify their view that therefore in order to have an equitable balance, there shouldn't be any Muslims on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subsequent to the preparation and submission of your report, have you come across or have you had cause to look into any further matters that would in any way alter your view or change anything that you have placed in that report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Well, having written the report and filed it, I then simply carried on working in the theatre for another year and a bit, and without actually going back to the region or looking at these particular events again, nothing that I learned over the subsequent year would lead me to change my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McLeod. That concludes my questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Counsel Pavkovic, who is going to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Counsel Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac will cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecution exhibit will be 393, Prosecution Exhibit 393.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, your Lordships. In this annex marked Annex R, it is evidently a report submitted by the U.N. and the ECMM. Cross-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the integral versions of these reports? These reports are referred to in Annex R on your report.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: If I understand the question correctly, you're asking whether this is the verbatim text of the original reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, not whether it is verbatim, but is it the integral version of the report? Is it the full text of the report for these days? You're covering the period between the 13th of April until the 30th of April. I'm asking if these are full texts of these reports.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No. What I was doing was taking full daily reports or weekly reports which would have a wide range of information, some of it administrative, to do with the ECMM, for example, and then highlighting those elements of the reports which were relevant to building up a picture of what had happened. So I think it's safe to say that these were all of the key elements which were reported by ECMM and UNPROFOR but certainly not all the information in the reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are the key events, in your view, in your eyes, is it, because you made the selection?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think these are all the items -- I think these are all the items which were reported, other than, for example, administrative matters. It's rather difficult, without having originals here, to be able to make a comparison, but I think that is the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that report, you cover a period -- you're covering the latter half of April; is that so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the report opens with an event in Travnik, where a conflict broke out between the HVO and the BH army, in the centre of the town. That is what it says. When you say here, if you look at the 13th of April, you say, "Uncontrolled forces within the HVO and the BH fought in the centre of the town or clashed in the centre of the town." Does that "BH" mean the army of BH?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the text, is it whenever you mention "BH", referring to some military formations, you mean the BH army; is that so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that day, it was reported that four HVO officers were abducted in the Travnik area, allegedly by members of the 7th Muslim Brigade; is that so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the 15th of April, 1993, in Zenica, a rather important meeting was held related to the security in the town and the investigation related to the abduction of HV officers. Why is it that Zivko Totic's abduction and the murder of his escorts are not mentioned here? You must have heard or read that Zivko Totic was the HVO commander in Zenica, that he was abducted on the 15th of April, and that his escorts were killed.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I had heard about that, but that was not one of the items in the reports which were written by ECMM or UNPROFOR. So I was aware of the event, people were certainly talking about it, but it didn't occur in the reports which I was going through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, on the 15th of April, there came the report of the shelling of Putis in the Busovaca municipality, an incident in Kacuni, and on the 15th of April, fierce fighting broke out in the area of Vitez. That is what your report says. After that, after a period of time, several reports come in covering the 16th of April, saying that there is fierce fighting in villages around Vitez, Rijeka, Vranjska, among the villages mentioned, and then they describe fighting around the sports stadium in Vitez and some combat activities in Gornja Veceriska. Also on the 17th of April, there is a report that ECMM is reporting about some combat activities in Vitez which lasted almost throughout that particular day. Now, in view of these reports that you went through and singled out, and in view of the interviews that you had with a large number of people, did you come to the conclusion that the BH army was present in the Lasva Valley on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. It was quite clear that the two parties had been working together, that a degree of tension had then built up. This had broken down into fighting, I believe, in the October of the year before. Then again in January of that year, tension was clearly very high and there were, as you have highlighted, a number of incidents going on in the days leading up to the 16th. And then on the 16th, the -- if you like, the pace of the battle changed, it accelerated, and what had been serious tension -- it was clear that people had been digging trenches, for example, in villages leading up to that point and people had been trying to restabilise it, that all of that broke down for a few days. And then, as you can see at the bottom of that page, are three -- or over the next page, that there was a ceasefire then signed on the 20th. So for about four days, there was intense fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So you concluded that it is beyond dispute that the BH army was in the Lasva Valley on the 16th of April, 1993, that they were in Vitez and around Vitez?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, and I saw members of the BiH just outside Vitez and in Stari Vitez, for example. So, yes, they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of these developments, isn't it true that on the 20th of April, a ceasefire was signed, and does this mean, in your view, that the BH army was quite strong in that area, that is, forces were quite strong in that particular area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, and indeed it was, as it says in my report, the view of Colonel Blaskic that if there had not been a ceasefire between -- brokered by the ECMM and UNPROFOR between the two parties, then the Muslim forces would certainly have cut off, in his view, the road between Vitez and Busovaca, and he was not quite sure what would have happened thereafter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, therefore, that the BH army forces were stronger than the HVO forces? You are saying that one doesn't know what could have happened had it not been for the ceasefire. Is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think Colonel Blaskic had been surprised by the strength of the, in my view, counterattack. In any case, he had been surprised by the strength of the attack which the BiH forces were able to launch against his troops following the 16th. That was the impression I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you believe General Blaskic at that moment, when he told you that, about the strength of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I made a value judgement about the strength of the army, but I certainly recognised that his description of what had happened and his evaluation of the tactical situation was almost exactly the same as that which UNPROFOR had given me a couple of days before. So what he was saying matched almost exactly what UNPROFOR had thought as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to have a look at the annex to your report relative to the conversation with the then Major Bryan Watters. Let me just find it. It is annex J. You met him on the 9th of May, 1993. Have you found the text?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you had a long conversation with Major Watters about the events of the 16th of April and the following days. You do not have your conversation recorded here in detail, but you drew four principal conclusions from what he told you; is that so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think these were his four conclusions which I noted, rather than my four conclusions. Certainly, his second point was his view, and I had no way of recognising whether that was true or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So when you go to the first item, it says there -- he speaks about the attacks on Stari Vitez, Vitez, Kruscica, and Ahmici and that these attacks were coordinated, or, rather, looked coordinated and that they were all carried out by the HVO. That is something that we also saw in your report, so you took over his conclusion. Under 2, it says that it seems that Ahmici was a very carefully chosen target because of the determination of the holy land and because there was a large number of imams there. Did you hear this conclusion or this definition from anybody else but Major Watters?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm afraid that now, six and a half years later, I simply can't remember whether anybody else had mentioned that. He certainly is the only person that I have noted in my report, from memory, as having said something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not hear from anyone else that Ahmici was attacked for religious reasons, to destroy houses of worship or to destroy a village which had a particular religious significance?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No, I can't remember anybody else saying that, although clearly Major Watters must have heard it from somebody or other people. But, no, I can't remember anybody else saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the third conclusion, it is said that Croats evidently demonstrated the intent of removing the Muslim population from Vitez but that they were not prepared for the quick and efficient response of the BH army. This is what you told us, that the BH army was in the Lasva Valley and that, evidently, according to Major Watters, it responded very well to the Croat attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. That was his view and the general consensus which UNPROFOR and ECMM seemed to have reached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fourthly, according to him, the HVO escaped, the HVO was saved only owing to the ceasefire concluded, owing to the good offices of the U.N. and the ECMM. That was the fourth conclusion.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That was his fourth conclusion. It was also a conclusion that I had reached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean this also would tally with what General Blaskic told you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that means that the HVO forces were evidently weaker or less strong than the BH forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I simply don't know how many troops there were on both sides, but it was clear at that tactical moment that the -- or it appeared clear at that tactical moment that the ABiH were reacting more forcefully and being more successful. That was the impression which one got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the BH army have enough troops in that area to launch an attack; that is, could it launch an attack, an attack on the Croats, on the HVO?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could the usher please show the witness P92? Could P92 be shown to the witness so that I can find it? Excuse me. P82; it is P82. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a report by the Human Rights Commission. It was drawn up at about the same time when your report was done, and it was based on the conclusions of Payam Akhavan and [redacted]. Are you familiar with that report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen this before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you met Payam Akhavan and [redacted] at the time when you were in Bosnia, in May 1993? Did you meet them then?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work together, or, rather, did you meet with the same people or similar people and cover similar topics? Did you also exchange your views or the news that you had received, or the information that you had received, did you exchange with them?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I met [redacted] before I went down to the Lasva Valley, and it was his intervention with the deputy head of the ECMM, which, in part, led to my being sent down there to see what had gone on. I think that both of them were present in Ahmici when I was there on the 4th of May, and I then bumped into the two of them again from time to time when I was working for the International Conference because they had an office in the compound. But I'm not sure that I actually met them again while I was in Vitez, I simply can't remember, in Vitez and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do remember being with them in Vitez on the 4th of May, 1993? In Ahmici, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who else was with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: So there were, I think, three ECMM ambassadors who were doing an even more rapid report than I was doing who were there, and they went to Vitez, Ahmici, and then they went straight down to Mostar where things were also bubbling over; Bob Stewart, who was providing the security; I think that Payam and [redacted] were there; certainly, one of them -- I think [redacted] was -- I think both of them were there; Jean-Pierre Thebault, who was hosting the ECMM ambassadors; and I was very much in the background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a SkyNews TV team with you also on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was behind such a high level visit to Ahmici? Who organised it and what was the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that Bob Stewart had organised it. I'm simply not sure now whether Jean-Pierre Thebault had asked for the ECMM ambassadors to be allowed to visit Ahmici. I think that that was probably the case, but I'm simply not sure what arrangements had been made, since I arrived the night before and this was my first day in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, were some human remains found in one of the houses and whether then it was recorded on tape?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did [redacted] say then that there were human remains in the house and that one should go there, see what it was about, and record it? Do you remember that, that he was referring to the communication from a witness from whom he had heard that it was his family there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that [redacted] knew that there was a house, and having walked up to the top of the village, we then walked down through the village, and he was attempting to find the house. They then located the house and a number of people, including, I think, the ECMM ambassadors, and Bob Stewart and [redacted] went into the house. I felt that there was no need to go and look myself at something quite as horrific as that, so I didn't go into the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see there, after you entered it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go into the house because I didn't particularly want to see human remains that had been burnt. I stood next to the cattle barn, which was actually outside the house, and one of the cows had obviously been burnt, so it was still quite smelly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you kindly to have a look -- even though you did not see this report, but it refers to the same period of time and the same area -- to look at item 9, segment B. It says: "The town of Vitez." Will you please have a look or, rather, read that passage?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not sure how much you'd like me to read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only this fragment, where it says: "Early in the morning on the 16th of April, armed conflicts broke out between the BH army and Croat HVO forces in the town of Vitez." I believe you agree with this wording. That is what you confirmed to us, that there is no doubt that there was an armed conflict between the BH army and the Croat forces in the town of Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is also said that there was a simultaneous and, obviously, concentrated attack of Croat forces on adjacent villages. You will agree with that too, won't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it was the translator or perhaps going from English to Croatian and back again, but in the original report, it's a concerted, rather than a concentrated attack, and therefore concerted would be coordinated. But basically I would agree with what's written.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it says that it seems that the majority of villagers managed to put up a defence, that fighting went on and lasted for a while, with the exception of Ahmici which is referred to later. Would you agree with this part too, that is, that the majority of villagers managed to fend off?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that in many cases, and I saw a couple of villages, there was fighting which had gone to and fro, and in some cases, the ABiH had mounted an offence and, therefore, was still actually there and present, and it did seem that Ahmici had been completely run over. I'm not sure to what extent there had been a defence, but as I described earlier on, the majority of bullet holes appeared to be and the destruction appeared to be of Muslim houses rather than the Croat houses, which were still intact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There's been a misunderstanding. I just wanted to ask you whether you agree with the statement made that most villagers managed to defend themselves and that fighting was still going on in those villages. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: By the time that I was there, the fighting had largely stopped because a ceasefire had been signed. I'm not sure when this report was written, but again there had been fighting. Many of the villages remained under either Muslim or Croat control, depending on which side was in control. Ahmici seemed to be different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. There's another sentence. I'm going to read it to you in the original because there's a problem with a bit of the translation of this text, but I would like you to read it just in case. It reads as follows: "... it seems to have changed hands, although the town of Vitez is now split by the confrontation line between the two forces which runs through it." So do you agree that it is primarily in those areas where a certain party had a majority, that that particular side managed to keep that area; that is to say, Muslims managed to keep under their control where they had a majority and the Croats managed to keep those territories where they had a majority, again with the exception of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not sure in practice, given what various people had said, whether a number of Croatian villages were lost on the original contact line, as the Muslims had pushed further south to try and cut the road -- that would be a possibility -- but, in principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of the village of Poculica, a Croat village, a village with a Croat majority before the war? There is a report of the ECMM stating that there is a prison somewhere in the area of Poculica where there are Croat detainees and that nobody has had access or control over that. Have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Forgive me. Since it's such a long time, is that one of the things that's referred to in the back of my report?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. At any rate, from this part of the report of the Human Rights Commission, you mainly agreed with this, didn't you, with a few exceptions on the Croat side and the village of Ahmici? This means that villagers were defending themselves, that there was a village defence that was organised in various villages; that is to say, that there were some BH army forces in these villages, is that correct, or, rather, any other military organisations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Without referring back to this report, which I'm not sure actually states it, I think that I'm quite clear that on both sides, villages were generally defended, and one could see this pattern of digging trenches around villages and then refilling trenches around villages. That was just the pattern of the war as it was progressing over those months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Trenches are not sufficient to defend a village. People are needed too. So there was some kind of a defence in every village, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. By saying the trenches were dug, I was implying that, therefore, people had dug the trenches and were then sitting in the trenches with their weapons to defend the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period that refers to an earlier stage, but we don't agree on all points. However, we do agree that there was a defence. Do you agree that in Ahmici, there was no defence, and was that the only village in the territory of the Vitez municipality that had no defence whatsoever and that that is why what happened in Ahmici happened, that is to say, the crime in Ahmici? What was the position of Ahmici? In your opinion, in view of all these other villages and all these other examples, was there a defence in Ahmici as well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not certain, since I was there after the events took place. I can't imagine that there was no defence of Ahmici. All I can conclude is that the defence of Ahmici was not as robust as in other places. I have no idea why that might have been the case, but I find it hard to imagine that there would have been no defence of the village, given the events which I could see everywhere else. But, clearly, whatever happened there overwhelmed whatever defence there might have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. There's also a factor of surprise, and other military factors that I wouldn't want to go into, that could be involved, but you believe that there was a defence, don't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have completed this part now, but I'd just like to go into a few other things. Mr. McLeod, I would be interested in the following: You said that the objective of your trip and the objective of your investigation was to ascertain what happened in the second half of April 1993. You are referring to the 16th only, but your report shows that you actually covered a longer period, that is to say, the entire second half of April.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Sorry. There was a question there. The 16th of April was clearly the trigger which set off a series of events. I went down to find out why that event had taken place. In order to understand that, one had to try and understand the context in which those events had taken place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your task was probably to give a report on inter-ethnic relations and the conflicts in Vitez, Busovaca, and Zenica in April 1993; at least, that is the title of your report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you talked to a large number of persons belonging to various structures. You also said that you received information from the military authorities, the political authorities. I wonder if you checked these data.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No. By and large, what I had was various bits of paper which were given to me, and in order to give as full a picture as possible, as rapidly as possible, I think I kept just about everything that I was given and attached it to the report, but given the time, it was impossible to actually verify most of what I was given, and I hope that that was clear from the way I described my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that one of the reasons why you concluded that the 16th of April involved an attack of Croats, the HVO, on the BH army was the fact that 13 prominent members of the Muslim community in Vitez were arrested. I can't find this now. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That is correct, and I think you'll find the list you're looking for at A2-1, so that's appendix 2 to annex A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These pages are marked in a strange way, I think, so that's why I have a problem all the time. The report shows that you talked to Hasan Sadibasic. He was the only person that you talked to, is that right, out of the 13 Muslims arrested; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No. I believe that I actually met some of these gentlemen in the prison in Busovaca, although at this stage, to go back and cross-reference between the list of people that I met in Busovaca and this list would take a couple of minutes. We could do that if you wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in the following: You met Sadibasic at his home. He had been released; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you check these other people out? In view of their importance and in view of the significance of this information, did you try to establish contact with these other persons mentioned in the list?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: With the exception of meeting some of them in the prison, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here that Munib Kajmovic, president of the SDA in Vitez, was also arrested on that occasion. Did you believe that piece of information?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think so at the time because that's what I was told. I think it's quite clear that under the circumstances, one couldn't be aware of whether everything one was being told was correct or not, which is why I tended to write everything down and present it so one could later on draw a conclusion when one had better facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked to Santic, who was the mayor of Vitez, and Pero Skopljak. You were told that they were trying to organise a meeting with Munib Kajmovic, who was president of the SDA in Stari Vitez. This was a man who had actually never been arrested. Did you put the two facts together?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We heard the testimony of a certain witness the other day, for example, that Batija Sivro, as member of the war presidency, was arrested on the 19th, the 19th of April, 1993, not, as it says here, on the 16th of April. The same goes for Nedim Zlotrg. I wonder if this changes your perception or your conclusion that the attack took place in the early morning and that obviously it was an attack of the HVO against the Muslim forces, if all of this is not correct, that is to say, if these Muslims were arrested three days later, after the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: My understanding is that if not all, then a majority of these people were arrested early in the morning on the 16th. If that is correct, and I suspect that you have far better ability to verify whether it is or not than I do, then my conclusion holds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So this is a conclusion on the basis of the facts as they were presented to you and that you did not check out. I'm also interested in the meetings that you had with some of these persons. First of all, you mentioned that you met the mayor of Zenica, Besim Spahic. You talked to him about the situation in the area and you got his description of the events after the 16th of April, 1993. Tell us briefly, so that we don't go into all of these details now, how did he describe the situation, that is to say, the position of the Croats from the 16th of April, 1993 onwards, that is to say, until you had this conversation with him on the 15th of April, 1993? What was the position of Croats in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: There had been tension. There was fighting going on. A large number of Croats who had been within the HVO in Zenica had been arrested. A number of them were still being detained. A number of -- a significant, I think, number of people had been either moved out or had left their houses. A number of houses had been destroyed, things had been stolen, and clearly this was a far-from-imperfect [sic] situation. What he said he was trying to do about it was that he was trying to stabilise the situation. He was trying to arrange joint patrols to go out and monitor events, and he was trying to encourage people to go back to their houses. So therefore the impression was that things were far from right and a number of things had taken place which were clearly wrong, but he was attempting to stabilise the situation. What he said he wanted was to return to a multi-ethnic community. That was what he was saying he was trying to achieve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In his report, it says that 2.000 people had fled -- this is concrete data related to what you had said -- that after the conflict 40 Croat houses were torched and looted, that 16 persons were killed, but not in a massacre. That is to say that there is quite a bit of information related to this very bad position of the Croats in Zenica. Is it your assessment that the Croats in Zenica at that time felt unsafe and insecure and that they thought that it was not safe for them to remain there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that quite clearly the Croatian population in Zenica had felt very insecure. As you can see further on in the report, I had a very difficult public meeting with a group of Croats just outside Zenica who were quite concerned. You can see the details that I was given by the two priests that I met, and so it was quite clear that the Croatian population in Zenica were unhappy, were not completely confident. But again the impression that I was given by the two priests was that things were trying to get back to normal and that they were trying to get access and were being given some access to the prisons, and that bit by bit, the local authorities were attempting to stabilise the situation. I would certainly not characterise it as being perfection, and I would not attempt to hide the fact that things were done to the Croatian population which were quite wrong; not at all. That's why I included all the information I was given by the priests, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the reports that were given to you by these priests, there is a meeting with Father Stjepan on the 7th of May, 1993. It says that 21 young men were missing; that they were not in prison; that they were probably in the music school; no one had access to the music school; it was under the authority of the 7th Muslim Brigade, that's what it seems, and also some people were burned to their deaths in their houses in Miletici; 250 families went in Nova Bila and Grahovcici; that another 14 houses were burned; that during the night, people were being taken away, so I would be interested in the following. You said the situation was not all that bad, that efforts were being made to stabilise the situation. However, from this report, we can see that this was on a massive scale, and you said yourself that quite a few persons remained detained, that is to say, members of the HVO remained detained in the prison in Zenica. After all of that, there is your conclusion that the Croats moved out of Zenica only and exclusively for propaganda reasons. Do you think that it is really propaganda reasons that made Croats leave Zenica, not all these events?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The conclusion that I reached at the time was that the large majority of the people who were moving were moving clearly because what was going on was very unsettling. I would certainly not want to go through that myself, and I doubt that anybody here would. However, that there was a concerted effort being made to move a large number -- to persuade a large number of people to move, and at the time I believe that a large number of those people were actually attempting to get back to Zenica. This is something which Bob Stewart was aware of and the ICRC were aware of, as well as ECMM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me about these Croats that wanted to return to Zenica and could not have, probably due to propaganda reasons as well. Which Croats did you talk to? Who are these persons who told you that they wanted to come back and could not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I didn't speak to the people who were trying to come back, but I did speak to members of BritBat, who had been talking to them. Now, I'm afraid it's so long ago that I can't remember the precise details, but even at this length, that is an impression which is still quite firm in my mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you think that primarily the reasons for Croats to leave Zenica were of a propaganda nature and that they were not threatened to such an extent that they really had to leave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think what I said was that the majority of people or a large number of people were being moved amongst other things because of propaganda. I think it is quite clear that a number of people were being terrorised, some of them were killed, which is the most extreme form of terrorism, and that for that reason, some of them were leaving. I think there's no doubt about that whatsoever. But I do think that there was also -- the impression I was given and the conclusion that I reached, and therefore that's what I thought at the time, was that a large number of people moved, amongst other things, because there was propaganda being put out -- "propaganda" is possibly the wrong word. It's a very strong word. There were messages being sent out from Vitez, suggesting that people should move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps recall through which channels these messages were sent?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: At this stage, not precisely, but I imagine it would have been on the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, this is probably a convenient time for a break. Do you have many more questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good. So we'll take a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last question, Mr. McLeod, you answered had to do with the manner that propaganda was conducted among the Croat population in Zenica, and you said that you thought that it was done by radio. That was what you said. Did you trust, did you believe those priests you talked to during those meetings? Fra Bozo and Stjepan, you believed them, you trusted them, you believed what they said?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. I have no reason to think they were telling me other than what they thought was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report of the 8th of May, 1993, your interview with Fra Bozo, at the end of page 2, you said, and these are Father Bozo's words, that many people who did not have houses wanted to leave but that he was against it, that is, that Fra Bozo was against it, but that they were not getting any information from the local television and radio and that they were under a complete media blockade. That is E-2, bottom of page 2 of that meeting. So, evidently, the propaganda was not conducted in that way. These reports, the ECMM's and U.N.'s, show that some people try to go back to Zenica several times, but that return never took place. Do you know if those Croat refugees did go back to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No, I have no idea whether eventually they were able to get back or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the information you received about the status of Bosnian Croats in Zenica, I should like to know, how is it that you did not take note of this in your report? Why is it that in your report you did not say anything about the status, about the lot of the Croat population in that part of the Bosnian territory?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: In respect, I think I actually said in my report -- because as far as I was concerned, the entire document was my report -- exactly what I was told by the Croats I met on the Muslim side of Zenica. The conclusion that I reached, which is what was highlighted on the first page of my report, was who had started that particular round of events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't really mean to be boring, but just now, you said you did not know if any part of the Croat population returned to the territory of Zenica, that is, any one of that large group of people, and you said in your report, the fourth passage, that the majority of the Croat population went back to their homes in the Zenica municipality. So your report is not quite accurate, is it? You can see it also in the fourth passage of your report.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought that your question was referring specifically to the people that we were discussing earlier on who were being held outside Vitez, close to the BritBat camp which we had discussed. I refer back to our earlier conversation. I don't know whether those people actually managed to get back to Zenica. I apologise if I had misunderstood your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we were not talking about people who were near the BritBat. We were talking about people in Zenica, at least so far, and I ask you about them specifically. But tell me, please, at that time, you must have known already that there was a brief lasting conflict between the BH army and the HVO in Zenica on the 17th of April, 1993? You did learn about that, didn't you? On that occasion, the HVO surrendered and on that occasion also, HVO members were arrested. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to your interview with Mayor Spahic, you attached a conclusion which he made as the president of the wartime presidency. It is A-4. He says there that -- he orders there to set up joint checkpoints, joint patrols made of MUP, BH army, and HVO members. Don't you think that it is a rather strange conclusion, since at that time the HVO had already become by that time an illegal and adversary army whose officers had been captured? That is A-1 of the conclusions -- item 1, sorry, item 1 of the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Annex 1, I believe. I think that there were still -- I'm not quite certain, but I think that in the area to the northwest of Zenica, there was still some fighting going on, that there had still been some fighting going on. I think you're quite correct that the majority of the HVO had been arrested and were being held in prison; however, what I was told was that they were attempting to set up joint patrols to go out and monitor the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can one organise joint patrols if one of the armies is detained?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Well, I'd conclude that you let some of the people out of prison and say, "Right. Let's now go and carry out joint paroles." I can't remember exactly how it was working. There was a very strong impression that they were trying to set up joint patrols and that the ECMM were involved in this process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you think that they told you one thing and doctored their conclusions and said a different thing on the ground? Because from these reports, what transpires is from the time you talked to them, 450 HVO members were detained at the outset, another 280 were in prison, and it was Fra Bozo who told you that. So don't you think that they were saying one thing and doing a different thing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: They were saying one thing, they were doing something else, but I think they may have been attempting to do a third thing. Again, I'd have liked the benefit of having been there for a further month to see what actually happened thereafter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. But could you tell us, if you know -- you told us that you had been to the Kaonik prison and spoken to its administrator, Zlatko Aleksovski. Did you also visit prisons in Zenica at the time, that is, the penitentiary, the music school, and the police prison?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: In practice, members of the ECMM had been into one of the prisons, the details of which are noted in the report, I believe, and I suspect that had I pushed, I would have had the opportunity to do it. In practice, I was running out of time. What I did do was present a case to the ABiH, which suggested that they would have a better negotiating position if they started to unilaterally release prisoners rather than holding prisoners, and this, indeed, is what they did. Again, the details of that are contained in the report, and the release of prisoners by the ABiH was witnessed by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked to Hadzihasanovic, the BH 3rd Corps commander, and it was on the 7th of May, 1993. One of the topics addressed there was access to prisons for your organisation, the ECMM, and priests. Hadzihasanovic said that he knew nothing about those prisons, such as the music school or the police, so, evidently, you did ask to be given access to those prisons.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. The issue was simply having enough time to physically do that while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it doesn't transpire from this that you were granted access to them. It even says that the 3rd Corps commander knew nothing about those prisons, that those prisons existed. Could you please look at D-1? Could you look at D-1, the contents of that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not curious about their denial of the existence of the prisons? Because you must have heard from Croats that they existed, that in the music school, there were Croats detained, that the conditions there were very bad, and that also there were cases of very serious harassment, ill-treatment of Croats there. Didn't that make you wonder?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It was precisely because we had heard that people were being detained in these places that we asked for access to them. I'm not sure whether I would be surprised at him saying that they didn't exist or not. The fact of the matter was that we were pressing to get access to what was clearly there, and again I'm not sure whether later on, during the following weeks, my colleagues at ECMM were actually able to get access. What I do know is that members of the ECMM and the priests did have access to the main prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who had the control over the music school, who had it under his control? Was it the police, was it the BH army, was it parts of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we actually established that. I know that there was a debate going on as to whether it was controlled by 7th Muslim Brigade, and there was also a debate going on as to whether they were controlled by the ABiH directly or not. And it's clear from what -- this little bit of the report says that Hadzihasanovic was attempting to distance himself from it. Again, in practice, I'm not sure exactly what the chain of command was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to your meeting with Hadzihasanovic, there is one thing which raises doubts. He says that he would like the 7th Muslim Brigade to be under the BH army control. Does that mean that the 7th Muslim Brigade was not under the BH army's control and that it was an army unto its own?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: As I said, there was a debate within the ECMM, as far as I can remember, about exactly what the chain of command was. Clearly, what he was attempting to say was that they were not under his control. I don't know -- I suspect that it would be easy enough to establish, but I simply don't know whether that was a fact or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you know who were members of the 7th Muslim Brigade and where was it quartered, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Again, I don't know precisely. I seem to remember that the discussion was that they were sitting -- people suggested that they were sitting in the music school and that perhaps there were members of the Mujahedin being part of that formation. But, again, these were what other people were saying. I'm not sure I've actually met anybody from 7th -- excuse me, 7th Muslim Brigade to establish whether that was a fact or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It also says here -- that is, Hadzihasanovic says that he wants the 7th Muslim Brigade under his control and that the Mujahedin are not under control. Have you come across the term "Mujahedin" or did you meet any people going by that name in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: People certainly talked about the Mujahedin as being a group or groups in Central Bosnia at the time. I don't think that I ever met anybody that either claimed to be or that I would term as being Mujahedin. It was one of those things that was fairly hard to try and verify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hadzihasanovic says that the Mujahedin are one of the uncontrollable groups. Did Croats mention the Mujahedin to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm sure that they did, and I suspect that you probably have a reference in my report which I can't remember at this stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also tell us, apart from these two priests, Father Stjepan and Father Bozo, which other Croats did you meet and talk to? Did you try to talk to HVO commanders in Zenica, perhaps, or representatives of political structures in Zenica, because I see that on several occasions the mayor mentioned the HDZ president to you, President Sakic, and according to Besim Spahic, he asked to be detained, to be arrested. That is what your report says, annex A-2, page 2. Did you talk to those people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that you gained an objective picture of all the developments without talking to all the representatives of the political or military power there in an area which was the object of your research?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that under the circumstances and given the time constraints in which I was operating, I produced a reasonable report. That's for various other people to judge. I certainly regret not meeting some of the personalities that would have been able to give further insight. But under the circumstances, I did the best that I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you talked to several people on several occasions, and my only question is how is it that you never met with the Croat political people there, because on the Muslim side you met with several people on several occasions, and that is why I'm asking you that. But just a few things more related to your visit in Stari Vitez. You were there, weren't you? You did go there once; at least that is what your report says.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Stari Vitez, did you see any houses destroyed or damaged?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. On the contact line between Stari Vitez and the rest of the town, there was significant battle damage to buildings on the perimeter, so one noticed that when you drove into the enclave and then again on leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these were the contact lines of Stari Vitez, and presumably the Croat part of Vitez, you are talking about the bordering areas, about the border area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I seem to have lost the translator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of damage -- I'm sorry -- what kind of damage did you see from firearms? I'm asking what kind of damage did you see on those houses in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: There was clearly damage from shooting, small-arms fire and machine guns, and I'm sure there's a video somewhere which would actually show you more accurately than my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So houses were damaged during armed conflict, isn't it, so marks of infantry weapons? There was no arson?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I can't remember seeing shell holes, although there were numerous reports, and some were included, I think, in my report, of the fact that Stari Vitez was being attacked with mortar and artillery fire. So I can't actually remember seeing a shell hole. It was the case that Stari Vitez was being shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was there damage in other parts of Vitez? I mean were houses in other parts of Vitez damaged too? As far as you could see, of course.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It would be far easier if you could get hold of some of the SkyNews video. However, there was certainly a lot of damage on the outskirts, and then as one drove through the town, it was clear that you were crossing a contact line or what had been a contact line, because there was a lot of battle damage, craters in the road and so on. I'm not sure that there was battle damage around the Croatian military headquarters that I went into, which was in the middle of the town. And then driving out to the southwest, again it was clear that one went across a contact line as one crossed from Croatian-controlled territory through to the village in the southwest that I visited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in Stari Vitez, did you see members of the BH army, do you remember seeing them, and do you also remember who you were staying with who you possibly talked to? Did you perhaps talk to any of the top military people in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I certainly saw armed soldiers in Stari Vitez, ABiH. I didn't actually go into the meeting that took place. I sat on top of a Mercedes and had a look to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also attended a meeting with Hakija Halilovic, commander of the 1st Battalion in Kruscica, on the 8th of May, 1993. Can you say -- that is Annex H, H-1. Can you say what it looked like? How was Kruscica -- or rather how many military men were there, and were there any trenches there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I can't remember seeing trenches. I probably met half a dozen or a dozen soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what happened to the Croat population in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I would imagine that they had left the village and moved into Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that that was also due to propaganda?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I have no idea. I would suspect that they decided it was the safest thing for them to do, under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. McLeod. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just have a few questions. Re-examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, we've heard reference to your seeing troops of the ABiH in Stari Vitez. Did you see troops in other parts of the town of Vitez at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. The only other soldiers that I actually saw in Vitez then were Croatian military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give any indication of the respective numbers in Vitez, taking account of Stari Vitez as well? Was one or another force predominant in numbers?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm quite sure that the Croatian military were in the majority in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've described what -- in your report, you refer to the action by the Croatian forces. Can you offer us any further information as to the facts upon which you were able to ascertain and form a view that the first strikes came from that side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Parties on both sides said that the other side had started it. A number of people gave fairly lucid descriptions of what had happened, suggesting that either they had been caught in their beds asleep or, indeed, they had been caught in their beds asleep by the other side. The U.N. observation posts, I think, were fairly clear about when fighting had started, because they had reports, they could hear what was going on, so there's no doubt about what time events started because you could hear the gunfire, I assume. I think that the U.N. reports were fairly clear, where they could see it, about who seemed to be attacking whom. In terms of who actually started things in Vitez and in Ahmici, since one has opposing views on both sides, from my point of view the most compelling evidence would be the fact that people appeared to be being arrested in the morning, and as I've said a number of times, I'm not quite sure that I can tie that back to a surprise attack by the Muslims on the Croats since there were a large number of Muslims who were arrested by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can move on from that, you've also referred to the actions of the Bosnian army as being a counterattack. Is there anything further you can add in that respect as to why you say that was specifically a counterattack?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think it was the conclusion which had been drawn by BritBat and my discussions with them, and it was also that the nature of what happened was consistent with the story that I was given by Colonel Blaskic, in terms of the way that they had responded, the only difference with his story being that as far as he was concerned, they had actually started, so he said it had been an attack as opposed to a counterattack. If my conclusion is correct, then clearly it was a counterattack rather than an attack. If my conclusion is wrong, then it could have been an attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
